title: Hereditary diseases: chromosomal diseases, gene diseases and diseases with hereditary predisposition. Types of marriage. Medical genetic counseling

goals.text: To teach the student the classification of hereditary diseases, the causes, signs and diagnosis of syndromes caused by changes in the number and structure of autosomes and sex chromosomes, hereditary metabolic diseases, multifactorial diseases, the medical genetic consequences of consanguineous marriage and the principles of medical genetic counseling (MGC).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the classification of hereditary diseases (chromosomal, gene, multifactorial, mitochondrial);
the karyotype and main signs of Down, Edwards, Patau, Klinefelter and Shereshevsky-Turner syndromes;
hereditary disorders of the metabolism of amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids and purines;
the concepts of genocopy and phenocopy, inbreeding and outbreeding;
the aim and stages of MGC and the levels of genetic risk.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify a syndrome from its karyotype formula;
calculate the proportion of shared genes from the degree of kinship;
assess the recurrence genetic risk for a family.

blocks.text: **Hereditary diseases** are diseases caused by changes in the hereditary apparatus (gene, chromosome, genome) that can be passed on to the next generations. They may be congenital or may appear later (for example, Huntington disease at the age of 35–45). A **congenital disease** is not always hereditary: congenital defects also arise from intrauterine infection or teratogens.

sections.title: 2. Syndromes caused by changes in the number of autosomes

blocks.title: Table 9.2. Autosomal trisomies
head: Syndrome
Karyotype

Main signs
rows: Intellectual disability, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthus, flat face and occiput, large tongue, short neck, transverse palmar crease, muscle hypotonia, heart defects, predisposition to leukemia
Low birth weight, dolichocephaly, small lower jaw, low-set malformed ears, overlapping flexed fingers (finger II over finger III), “rocker-bottom” feet, heart defects; most die before 1 year

parts.text: The main risk factor for Down syndrome is **maternal age**: at 25 years the risk is ≈ 1 : 1250, at 35 years ≈ 1 : 350, at 40 years ≈ 1 : 100, at 45 years ≈ 1 : 30. In the **translocation** form (for example, a Robertsonian translocation of chromosome 21 onto chromosome 14) one parent is a balanced translocation carrier and the recurrence risk is high, so the parents’ karyotype is examined.

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Palm dermatoglyphics: a — normal palm print; b, c — the single transverse (“simian”) crease and altered papillary patterns in Down syndrome (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In Down syndrome, besides intellectual disability, there are **congenital heart defects** (in 40–50 % of patients, most often atrioventricular canal), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, reduced immunity, a 10–20-fold increased risk of **acute leukaemia** and early **Alzheimer's disease** after age 40 (an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21). With early rehabilitation and surgical correction of heart defects the average life expectancy has increased to 60 years.

head: Form
Origin
Risk for the next child
rows: Non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in meiosis (usually maternal, meiosis I)
Chromosome 21 is joined to chromosome 14 by a Robertsonian translocation
Non-disjunction in mitosis after cleavage of the zygote

parts.text: A carrier of a **balanced translocation** (45 chromosomes but complete genetic material) is healthy, but some of his or her gametes are unbalanced. So in recurrent miscarriage, stillbirth or the birth of children with Down syndrome, **the karyotypes of both parents** are examined.

blocks.text: **Syndromes caused by changes in chromosome structure:** **cri-du-chat** syndrome (46,5p^−^ — deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5): the infant’s cry resembles a cat’s mewing (underdeveloped larynx), microcephaly, moon face, hypertelorism, severe intellectual disability. **18q^−^ syndrome** (deletion of the long arm of chromosome 18): intellectual disability, microcephaly, facial and ear anomalies. **Wolf-Hirschhorn** (4p^−^), **Williams** (7q11.23 microdeletion) and **DiGeorge** (22q11.2 microdeletion) syndromes also belong to this group.

Main features

blocks.text: Chromosomal abnormalities cause ≈ 50 % of early miscarriages: the most common among them are autosomal trisomies (especially trisomy 16), 45,X and **triploidy** (69,XXX or 69,XXY). In live-born babies the frequency of chromosomal diseases is ≈ 0,5–0,6 %.

parts.text: Common signs of chromosomal diseases: **multiple congenital defects**, delay of intellectual and physical development, a dysmorphic face (minor anomalies) and altered dermatoglyphics. The diagnosis is confirmed only by **karyotyping**. Most of them arise anew (de novo) and are not passed on, because patients are often infertile.

sections.title: 4. Gene (monogenic) diseases — hereditary disorders of metabolism

blocks.text: Most gene diseases are **enzymopathies**: as a result of a mutation an enzyme is not synthesized or its activity decreases, the preceding metabolites accumulate and have a toxic effect, while the next product is deficient. They are mostly inherited as autosomal recessive.

parts.text: Phenylketonuria, galactosemia and congenital hypothyroidism are detected by **newborn screening**: a drop of blood from the baby’s heel is tested. A special diet or hormone therapy started early (in the first weeks of life) prevents intellectual disability.

sections.title: 5. Diseases with hereditary predisposition. Genocopy and phenocopy

blocks.text: **Diseases with hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)** are produced by the sum of the small effects of several genes (a polygenic system) together with environmental factors. They are the most common (hypertension, atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, bronchial asthma, peptic ulcer, schizophrenia, psoriasis, many congenital defects). Typical features: clustering of the disease in families, but not in Mendelian ratios; the risk rises with closer kinship and with more affected persons in the family; prevention is possible by changing environmental factors (diet, smoking, stress).

Multifactorial diseases are explained by the **threshold model**: each person has a sum of predisposing genes and environmental factors — the **liability**; when it exceeds a certain threshold the disease appears. Therefore: (1) the risk for relatives of an affected person is higher than in the general population but does not fit Mendelian ratios; (2) the more affected relatives and the more severe the disease in the family, the higher the risk; (3) the risk is higher for relatives of a patient of the less often affected sex (for example, relatives of a girl with pyloric stenosis).

Definition
Example

sections.title: 6. Principles of treatment and prevention of hereditary diseases

blocks.text: Although a hereditary disease is linked to the genotype, many of its forms can be treated or made less severe. Methods of treatment:

blocks.title: Table 9.10. Methods of treating hereditary diseases
head: Method
Essence
Examples
rows: Removing from the diet the substance that forms a toxic metabolite
Phenylalanine-free diet in phenylketonuria, milk-free diet in galactosaemia
Giving the hormone, enzyme or protein
Thyroxine in congenital hypothyroidism, factor VIII in haemophilia, enzyme in Gaucher disease
Correcting a defect or transplanting an organ
Surgery for cleft lip and heart defects; bone-marrow transplantation in thalassaemia
Introducing a normal gene copy into cells with a viral vector or editing the gene
Spinal muscular atrophy, some immunodeficiencies, haemophilia

items: **Primary (before marriage and pregnancy)** — genetic counselling, carrier testing, pregnancy planning, folic acid, avoiding mutagens and teratogens, having children before the mother is 35.
**Secondary (prenatal)** — screening and prenatal diagnosis in pregnancy; if severe pathology is found, the family makes a decision.
**Tertiary (postnatal)** — newborn screening, early detection of disease and starting treatment before signs appear.

blocks.text: **Outbreeding** is marriage between unrelated persons; it reduces the probability that recessive alleles become homozygous and increases heterozygosity in the population. **Inbreeding** is marriage between relatives. Relatives may have received the same recessive alleles from a common ancestor, so such marriages increase the frequency of autosomal recessive diseases, congenital defects, stillbirths and miscarriages.

parts.text: In a marriage of first cousins the risk of a child with severe hereditary pathology is about 2 times higher (≈ 5–6 %) than the risk in the general population (≈ 3 %); if there is a recessive disease in the family, the risk is even higher. Such couples should definitely undergo genetic counseling.

blocks.text: **Medical genetic counseling** is specialized medical care aimed at preventing the birth of children with hereditary pathology. Its aim is to determine and explain the level of genetic risk to the family and to help it make a decision about having children. Counseling is **prospective** (before marriage or pregnancy, before an affected child is born) or **retrospective** (after an affected child has been born in the family).

items: a child with a hereditary disease or congenital defect in the family;
consanguineous marriage;
maternal age over 35;
recurrent miscarriage, stillbirth, infertility;
exposure to teratogenic factors (drugs, radiation, infections) during pregnancy;
high risk in prenatal screening.
**Clarifying the diagnosis** — clinical, cytogenetic, biochemical and molecular tests.
**Drawing a pedigree** and determining the type of inheritance.
**Calculating the genetic risk** (by Mendel’s laws or empirical tables).

**Conclusion and explanation** — the risk, the severity of the disease and the possibilities of treatment and prenatal diagnosis are explained to the family in plain words; the decision is made by the family.

Risk
Recommendation

skills.title: Skill: calculating the recurrence genetic risk in a family

items: Establish the diagnosis of the proband’s disease and its type of inheritance (pedigree, karyotype, biochemical analysis).
For a monogenic disease write the parents’ genotypes: in AR both Aa, in AD one Aa, in X-recessive the mother X^A^X^a^.
Calculate the risk by Mendel’s laws: AR — 25 %, AD — 50 %, X-recessive — 50 % for sons.
For a chromosomal disease examine the parents’ karyotypes: in simple trisomy the recurrence risk is low (≈ 1 % + age-related risk), in balanced translocation carriage it is high.
For multifactorial diseases use empirical risk tables.
Assign the risk level (low, moderate, high) and explain the possibility of prenatal diagnosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: When the patient’s karyotype was examined, some cells were found to be 45,X and others 46,XX.
cases.answer: This is mosaicism — 45,X/46,XX (the mosaic form of Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome). The zygote was normal (46,XX), but in one of the early cleavage divisions an X chromosome was lost (anaphase lag) or failed to separate, giving rise to two cell lines. The signs are usually milder than in the complete form of the syndrome, and some patients may be fertile.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A marriage of first cousins produced 2 children: one had developmental defects, the other severe intellectual disability.
cases.answer: First cousins share 1/8 of their genes, and the inbreeding coefficient of their children is 1/16: there is a high probability that both parents carry the same recessive allele from the common grandparents. As a result the children become homozygous (aa) for that allele and autosomal recessive diseases appear (for example, enzymopathies with intellectual disability such as phenylketonuria, or syndromes of congenital defects). Genetic counseling, clarification of the diagnosis and prenatal diagnosis are recommended before the next pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A child with a hereditary disease was born in a family that had undergone genetic counseling and in which an affected child was not expected.
cases.answer: Possible reasons: (1) a new (de novo) mutation or chromosomal error arose in a sex cell of one parent — such cases cannot be predicted in advance; (2) low risk does not mean zero risk — the probability was realized; (3) the disease was hidden in the family because of incomplete penetrance or genocopy; (4) germline mosaicism; (5) uncertain paternity or an incorrect diagnosis. The diagnosis of the new child must be clarified and the risk recalculated.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: The second child of a 25-year-old woman was born with Down syndrome; before that she had two miscarriages. The mother's karyotype is 45,XX,t(14;21). The father's karyotype is normal.
cases.ask: Which form of Down syndrome does the child have? Why did this happen even though the mother is young? What is the risk for the next child?
cases.answer: The mother is a carrier of a **balanced Robertsonian translocation**: her chromosome 21 is fused with chromosome 14, giving 45 chromosomes in total but complete genetic material, so she is healthy. Some of her gametes carry the fused 14/21 chromosome together with a free chromosome 21 — at fertilisation the child has three doses of chromosome 21 material (**translocation Down syndrome**, 46 chromosomes). Some gametes are unbalanced and monosomic embryos die — this explains the miscarriages. The risk does not depend on the mother's age; the risk of Down syndrome for the next child is ≈ 10–15 %, so prenatal diagnosis is recommended in every pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A woman whose first child was born with spina bifida is planning another pregnancy.
cases.answer: Neural tube defects are a **multifactorial** disease; after one affected child the recurrence risk is much higher than in the general population (≈ 2–5 %). Recommendations: (1) take **high-dose folic acid** at least 1–3 months before planned conception and throughout the 1st trimester (reduces the risk by ≈ 70 %); (2) control diabetes well if present, reduce obesity and avoid some anticonvulsants (valproate); (3) in pregnancy, measure maternal blood **α-fetoprotein** and do ultrasound (weeks 16–20) — early detection of the defect.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 40-year-old man has developed involuntary jerky movements and disturbances of memory and behaviour. His father had the same illness at this age. The patient has an 18-year-old son.
cases.ask: What disease should be considered? What is the son's risk and what ethical issues arise?
cases.answer: This is **Huntington's chorea** — an autosomal dominant disease caused by expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats in a gene on chromosome 4. It usually begins at 35–45 years, often after the person has had children. The patient is heterozygous, so his son's risk of inheriting the gene is **50 %**. The number of repeats may increase when passed from the father, leading to earlier onset (**anticipation**). DNA analysis can diagnose the disease before signs appear, but it cannot yet be cured; therefore presymptomatic testing is done only at the free wish of an adult and after psychological counselling.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Chromosomal diseases are confirmed by **karyotyping**, enzymopathies by **biochemical** and **molecular** tests.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Trisomy numbers: **“13 — Patau, 18 — Edwards, 21 — Down”** — the smaller the number, the larger the chromosome and the more severe the syndrome.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Newborn screening (PKU, hypothyroidism, galactosemia) and genetic counseling are the most effective prevention of hereditary diseases.
